Purpose This paper aims to advance strategic management theory by proposing iRBV – an Information Systems-based extension of the resource-based view (RBV) and capability-based view (CBV). This essay argues that globally available technologies fundamentally change the role of firm resources and capabilities, enabling firms not merely to respond to market conditions but to reshape the rules by which markets operate. Drawing on RBV and CBV, the author proposes iRBV as a framework for understanding how firms can adopt and adapt global technologies – such as artificial intelligence and blockchain – to internalise externalities and create new markets. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a viewpoint on how firms can proactively reshape their environment by incorporating externalities into their strategies. The author proposes iRBV – an information systems (IS)-based extension of the RBV, CBV and natural RBV – as a theoretical advancement that enables management scholars and practitioners to develop business models capable of addressing market externalities, including climate change, at the firm level. Findings Through two illustrative cases – ChatGPT and the Libra coin – this essay demonstrates how global technologies can enable firms to reshape markets and internalise externalities that lie beyond the scope of traditional RBV and CBV. Climate change mitigation is presented as one significant application of this mechanism. Research limitations/implications iRBV is presented as a theoretical provocation rather than a fully operationalised framework. Its primary limitation is the reliance on illustrative cases rather than systematic empirical evidence. Future research should develop the microfoundations of iRBV – specifically the routines, heuristics and higher-order capabilities that enable firms to adopt and adapt globally available technologies for externality internalisation. Additional boundary conditions require investigation, including the applicability of iRBV beyond digital technologies, the role of power asymmetries and path dependencies in capability activation and the conditions under which profit-maximisation logic aligns with – rather than diverges from – the internalisation of societal externalities. Practical implications iRBV equips managers with a theoretical lens for identifying externalities as strategic opportunities rather than regulatory obligations. Firms with strong IS capabilities – such as those already deploying artificial intelligence (AI) or blockchain – are well positioned to develop business models that internalise externalities while generating profit. iRBV encourages managers to incorporate a global view of their strategic environment into firm strategy, treating the internalisation of externalities not as a cost of doing business but as a potential source of market dominance. Social implications iRBV suggests that addressing societal externalities – including climate change – need not depend solely on top-down regulation or international agreements. By providing firms with a profit-driven mechanism for internalising externalities, iRBV enables a bottom-up approach in which individual firms take the lead in reshaping market rules and addressing global challenges. This shifts the locus of responsibility from governments and international bodies to firms themselves, driven by intrinsic strategic logic rather than external mandate. If widely adopted, iRBV could contribute to a broader transformation in how business and society relate to one another in the face of global challenges. Originality/value This paper advances RBV and CBV into iRBV, a theoretical extension that positions globally available technologies as levers for internalising market externalities through intrinsic, profit-driven firm strategies. Illustrative examples demonstrate how technologies such as blockchain and AI could enable firms to address climate change – including CO2 traceability, cryptocurrency-based climate incentives and environmentally-linked search restrictions – while simultaneously achieving market dominance.

Advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) produce synthetic human faces that are difficult to distinguish from photographs of real people. Because social impressions from faces form rapidly and can influence consequential judgements, the growing realism of AI-generated faces raises questions about how these faces are socially perceived. This review synthesises evidence from 10 empirical studies examining whether AI-generated faces are evaluated differently from real faces and what may account for these differences. Across the reviewed studies, AI-generated faces receive more favourable social evaluations than real faces, including higher ratings of trustworthiness and attractiveness, while familiarity also emerges as a component of their perception. These patterns are consistent with established face-perception research showing that faces perceived as more typical tend to receive more favourable social evaluations. AI-generated faces may disproportionately reflect such characteristics, including greater averageness or typicality. However, appearance alone does not determine these judgements: disclosure, labelling, and beliefs about artificiality can weaken or alter otherwise favourable impressions. Overall, social responses to AI-generated faces appear to reflect an interaction between perceptual characteristics and beliefs about origin. The central challenge is no longer only whether AI-generated faces can pass as human, but how people who do not exist can shape real social judgements.

documents.abstract: Scientific results produced by LLM-generated analysis code must be understandable and reproducible. However, uncertainty can arise at different stages of the process, both in the original natural language specification and in the generated implementation. As a result, even executable code may not provide a clear understanding of which quantities are being computed or which assumptions determine the final results. To address this challenge, we introduce quantity-grounded semantic differencing, a multi-agent framework for analyzing and comparing scientific programs generated by LLMs. The framework assigns code generation, execution, tracing, and validation to separate agents, allowing it to reconstruct how key output quantities are produced and to identify differences between the intended analysis and the implemented code. We also introduce a module that inspects ambiguities in the initial user instruction and suggests alternative rewrites before code generation. Its modular design is intended to facilitate application to different scientific domains by replacing domain-specific resources while preserving the same workflow. We validate the framework on representative collider physics analyses. In the studies HEP cases, the modular task decomposition provides explicit intermediate artifacts for inspection and the complete workflow was operated with substantially smaller models than in the previous implementation.

documents.abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research. Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) offers significant opportunities to support complex, time-critical decisions in intensive care units (ICUs). However, clinical adoption depends not only on predictive accuracy, but also on whether AI recommendations are visualised in formats that are interpretable, actionable, and trusted by clinicians. Poorly designed interfaces risk undermining usability, trust, and integration into workflows. This study investigates ICU clinicians' preferences for graphical user interface (GUI) design and explainability strategies in the AI Clinician, a reinforcement learning tool for sepsis management. Methods An online survey was conducted between November 2023 and November 2024 with 24 ICU clinicians from UK hospitals. Participants evaluated three GUI prototypes of the AI Clinician's treatment recommendations; 1) discrete numerical doses, 2) dose ranges, and 3) qualitative increase/decrease guidance. Clinicians rated each prototype's usefulness and ease of use using Likert scales, completed pairwise comparisons, and provided free-text feedback. They also ranked four types of AI explanations (treatment option gap, projected mortality, feature importance, and influential training examples) according to their perceived benefit. Descriptive statistics summarised quantitative data, while thematic analysis was applied to qualitative responses. Results Clinicians expressed a strong preference for the range-based prototype, which best balanced clarity with flexibility for patient-specific adjustments. Prototype 2 (ranges) achieved the highest ratings for meeting requirements (median = 6/7) and ease of use (median = 6/7) and was preferred in 77.3% of pairwise comparisons. Discrete numbers were considered precise but overly rigid, while qualitative increase/decrease guidance was simple but too vague for critical decisions. Treatment option gap (mean = 4.04) and projected mortality (mean = 3.71) were ranked most beneficial for explainability, although clinicians emphasised that multiple, complementary, explanations were necessary to enhance transparency and trust. Discussion The findings suggest that AI recommendations for sepsis management should be presented using range-based visualisations that reflect real-world clinical practice by supporting flexibility without sacrificing clarity. Multiple explanation types, particularly those tied directly to treatment rationale and patient outcomes, are essential for building trust. These insights highlight the importance of human-centred design, clinician involvement in development, and layered transparency to optimise AI clinical decision support systems in critical care.

documents.abstract: Industrial accidents triggered by natural events (Natech) are becoming more frequent in the context of climate change, highlighting the need to analyze these risks and integrate them into land-use planning (LUP) decision-making processes. In Romania, LUP relies on the combination of individual accident scenario frequencies and impact zones, overlapped with functional land-use categories. However, this approach does not integrate the vulnerability of the population, nor the individual risk (IR) associated with Natech accidents. This paper proposes improved LUP criteria, based on the assessment of social vulnerability to Natech accidents triggered by earthquakes, and the quantification of IR. First, the Natech Vulnerability Index (NVI) was developed, at local administrative unit level in a county with eleven Seveso sites, by the additive integration of the Social Seismic Vulnerability Index (SSVI) and the Technological Vulnerability Index (TVI). Second, a quantitative Natech risk analysis was performed for a pilot site, resulting the Natech IR levels. These combined with the NVI serve as a new decision-making criterion in the LUP process, highlighting the importance of social, natural and technological aspects. The methodology is adaptable also to other natural hazards by selecting the specific vulnerability indicators and the Natech risk analysis models.

documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) holds broad application prospects in medical education; however, systematic empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness in facilitating case discussions and virtual patient consultation remains scarce. This study recruited undergraduate medical students and conducted experiments to examine the pedagogical effects of AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation. Methods A total of 207 medical undergraduates participated in this study. Using the self-developed intelligent experimental platform, medical students engaged in AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation. Experiment 1 employed a single-factor, three-level between-subjects design to compare the effects of AI-assisted case discussion, peer case discussion, and a lecture-only control condition on medical students’ knowledge acquisition, intrinsic motivation, and interaction quality. Experiment 2 utilized a single-factor, four-level between-subjects design to examine the effects of virtual patient consultation and the sequencing of AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation on medical students’ knowledge acquisition, intrinsic motivation, and consultation process quality. The control group participants were the same individuals across both experiments. Results Results indicated that the AI-assisted case discussion group achieved significantly higher knowledge scores than the control group. The virtual consultation group, the consultation-then-discussion group, and the discussion-then-consultation group all outperformed the control group in knowledge acquisition. The discussion-then-consultation group demonstrated higher intrinsic motivation and consultation comprehensiveness, yet exhibited lower empathy than the virtual consultation group. Conclusions These findings suggest that both AI-assisted case discussion and virtual patient consultation can effectively enhance medical students’ knowledge acquisition compared with learning by watching instructional videos only, while different intervention sequences exert differential effects on intrinsic motivation, consultation comprehensiveness, and empathy. The results provide theoretical foundations and practical guidance for AI-empowered medical education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Scientific laboratories are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence tools, electronic laboratory notebooks, automated workflows, and digital twins. Yet, these typically operate as isolated components rather than as parts of a coherent laboratory-scale knowledge infrastructure. We use the term Epistemic Coordination Systems (ECS) to refer to the class of human-governed systems that coordinate laboratory memory, provenance, tacit knowledge, negative laboratory results, external evidence, AI-supported synthesis, verification status, and human judgment gates. The literature needed to conceptualize ECS exists but is fragmented across streams ranging from distributed cognition and transactive memory to retrieval-augmented generation, AI governance, and connected laboratories. This protocol specifies a scoping review with systematic mapping that will integrate these streams: eligibility follows a Population-Concept-Context framework centered on scientific laboratories; searches cover seven bibliographic and preprint sources plus official standards sources, with search strings calibrated against a documented 212-record seed corpus and peer reviewed before execution; screening proceeds in two stages, and a second reviewer independently re-screens at least 20 percent of records at each stage as a reliability check. From every included source, sixteen predefined data fields are extracted. Synthesis then produces four outputs: a map of the literature streams, a taxonomy of ECS components, distinctions between ECS and adjacent systems, and an initial set of design requirements and evaluation dimensions. Distinctively, the protocol is provenance-first: it applies to its own conduct the epistemic-coordination principles it studies, through bounded and non-binding AI assistance, human verification of every decision and claim, dedicated AI-provenance and human-override logs, and claim-source mapping. The protocol was registered before formal searches (OSF Registries; DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/WGMUY ; July 5, 2026).

As AI becomes embedded in organizational decision-making and knowledge production, employees gain new tools for accessing and generating information while also confronting concerns about algorithmic evaluation, data use, and accountability. Drawing on research on AI ethics, algorithmic management, and organizational creativity, this conceptual study defines organizational AI ethics governance as the rules, procedures, and allocation of responsibilities that guide the development, deployment, operation, and retirement of AI systems. We argue that such governance can shape employee creativity through several connected mechanisms. Fair and contestable procedures can strengthen procedural justice, while transparent system boundaries and meaningful human review can support calibrated trust. Tolerance for responsible experimentation, together with discretion over how AI is used, can protect psychological safety and job autonomy. Governance also determines whether human–AI collaboration broadens exploration or channels employees toward standardized outputs. These effects depend on task characteristics, the stakes of AI-assisted decisions, whether AI is used primarily for automation or augmentation, employees' AI literacy, and the consistency between formal rules and managerial conduct. This study suggests that organizations should translate ethical principles into risk-based review, purpose limitation in data use, effective contestability and appeal mechanisms, employee participation, and oversight across the AI system life cycle so that AI can serve as a resource for careful creative work rather than a substitute for judgment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Organizations that put algorithms into consequential decisions usually keep a person in the loop, on the assumption that the person adds something the model lacks. This paper checks that assumption against four bodies of published evidence: a meta-analysis of 106 experiments, field and trial evidence on judges, radiologists, physicians and consultants, a 2025 global survey of 1,993 respondents, and the oversight provisions of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act. Published effects are put on a common scale and a short decision model is derived to show when an override can pay. On average a human–AI combination does worse than the better of its two members (Hedges’ g = − 0.23, 95% CI − 0.39 to − 0.07), which corresponds to a 43.5% chance of beating it. The loss is concentrated in decision tasks ( g = − 0.27); in creation tasks the estimate is positive but imprecise ( g = 0.19, CI − 0.09 to 0.48). Relative capability matters most: combinations gain when the human alone is the stronger member ( g = 0.46) and lose when the algorithm is ( g = − 0.54). In the model, unrestricted overrides change accuracy by exactly the accuracy gap between human and algorithm, and with unequal error costs the human’s odds of being right must exceed the algorithm’s by the cost ratio. In the survey, respondents at high-performing organizations were 2.8 times as likely to report a defined human-validation process (65% against 23%; odds ratio 6.2), an association that is large but cross-sectional and self-reported. The evidence is highly heterogeneous ( I ² = 97.7%) and mostly predates current generative models. Oversight helps where it is built around what the human knows and the model does not, and not where it exists in name only.

Purpose This study explores the implications of artificial intelligence (AI) integration into business management practices, emphasizing its impact on intellectual capital components. Specifically, it examines how AI integration influences the interaction between human, structural and relational capital in managerial processes. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a rigorous thematic analysis conducted in NVivo. Data collected through an online qualitative questionnaire administered to managers from multiple sectors were analyzed to identify key dimensions of AI integration in business contexts and to develop a conceptual model explaining their interactions. Findings The findings reveal four key dimensions: the role of AI in managerial processes, the challenges associated with AI, the strategies and best practices required to integrate AI into management and the strategies needed to adapt and train human resources in organizations integrating AI. While AI enhances efficiency, automation and decision-making processes, sustainable integration requires strategic planning, gradual implementation and investment in human capital. Overall, AI integration appears to enhance the interaction between human, structural and relational capital rather than radically restructuring intellectual capital. Practical implications The link between technological implementation and human-centered challenges provides practical guidance for organizations undergoing digital transformation. Gradual AI integration through pilot projects, employee training and governance structures supports responsible human–AI collaboration and strategic decision-making. Originality/value This research extends the traditional technology–organization–environment framework by conceptualizing AI integration as a dynamic socio-organizational process. Furthermore, it highlights how AI-driven managerial practices reinforce existing intellectual capital and provides a conceptual model explaining these dynamics.

Generative AI has ended the assumption that unsupervised student work reflects a student’s own unaided thinking, forcing a return to first principles in assessment. This article uses The University of Sydney’s two-lane approach, which separates secure assessment of learning from open assessment for and as learning, to frame a practical account of putting AI into students’ hands. Drawing on ‘Dr MattTabolism’, an AI biochemistry tutor I built and deployed, and on a computational study of how students actually used it, I show a consistent gap between how such tools are designed and how they are used. Students largely sought answers rather than sustained dialogue, satisfaction did not correlate with improved learning outcomes, and usage concentrated around deadlines. How educators contextualised AI use affected learning more than how the tool behaved. I argue that this offloading is partly a product of over-assessment, and that formative, lower-stakes work remains essential precisely because it is where students can afford the desirable difficulties that learning requires. Reducing assessment load is a validity measure, not a soft option. I close with practical starting points for educators, framed around the pedagogical roles AI can play and the risks each carries, and the educator’s role as designer.

The promise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education has motivated a rapidly growing literature whose titles, abstracts, and keywords mention acceptance, attitudes, intention, or perception more than six times as often as self-regulated learning or metacognition. This critical review argues that research on GenAI in education is repeating the founding mistake of learning analytics, measuring what is easy to count rather than what matters for learning. Building on the COPES model of self-regulated learning, this paper develops the gradual reduction of AI delegation (GRAD) framework, in which GenAI performs, proposes, or prompts at eight task stages. Within GRAD, GenAI can take on operations essential to the learning goal. Such delegation helps rather than replaces learning only when the support fades as learners improve. For claims that GenAI improves learning, the paper proposes four validity criteria, namely unassisted outcomes, process evidence, calibration, and ideally gains that outlast the support.

documents.abstract: A Large Language Model (LLM), its harness, and the test-time compute budget jointly determine its behavior. Consequently, the same underlying model, embedded in different agentic workflows or allocated different amounts of test-time compute, can exhibit markedly different performance. Psychologists face an analogous challenge when evaluating human performance: the same person may behave differently under different incentives and levels of deliberation. Psychological tasks therefore provide an ideal testbed for studying such behavioral variation. However, when adapted to LLMs, these tasks are typically text-transcribed, replaying fixed, language-rendered experiments as static prompts. This format is ill-suited to agent evaluation, where actions can alter future observations and task states. Conversely, although dynamic environments are prevalent in the evaluation of LLM agents, they rarely ask whether the resulting behavior is human-like. Here, we bridge this gap by transforming psychological tasks into dynamic environments in which agents can interact and by using a learned human-policy model to evaluate how compatible the resulting behavioral trajectories are with human behavior. Across these environments, we find that this compatibility varies with an LLM's agentic configuration and the psychological task, and that memory raises it mainly by making choices more predictable rather than more human-like. These findings motivate a more holistic evaluation of LLM agents in psychology-inspired environments, accounting for both the backbone model and its agentic scaffold.

China’s government is making artificial intelligence (AI) a national development priority and is promoting its adoption across the country’s economy and society. This essay discusses how AI may affect China’s economy, specifically how it may challenge the performance-based legitimacy China’s government has depended upon over the last several decades. In particular, this essay shows how AI affects workers in different industries, workers at different stages of their careers, different age groups, and different geographic locations. Evidence suggests AI is driving down demand for routine tasks and certain forms of creative work and that wealthier, more economically diversified regions are better able to cope with the disruption. It also shows that feelings of insecurity are on the rise, as demand for entry-level workers may be decreasing and senior workers now confront a situation in which their junior counterparts can do some of their jobs. This essay also discusses opportunities arising from AI in the public sector, specifically how AI could help China’s economy by creating new industries and raising productivity and can help its government by improving the delivery of public services. Finally, this essay discusses how China’s government is trying to help people who have been directly and indirectly affected by AI through initiatives like employment programs, court rulings protecting employees, and monitoring of how the economic gains from AI are distributed. Although the evidence shows AI results in these labor market changes, whether they will undermine public trust remains a projection rather than an established fact.

The theories employed include Artificial Intelligence, encompassing the dimensions of AI Awareness, Perceived Quality, Perceived Authenticity, and Transparency, as well as the theory of Prospective Consumer Trust, encompassing Credibility, Benevolence, Integrity, and Purchase Intention. Using a quantitative approach with a survey method, the study population comprised 152 followers of the @filadelfiasushii Instagram account, with a sample of 110 respondents. The data analysis technique used was simple linear regression. The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has triggered an institutional crisis of academic trust. This challenge is characterized by an "adoption-trust paradox," where ubiquitous student usage coexists with deep ethical skepticism and concerns over academic integrity. While existing research predominantly focuses on individual technology acceptance models (e.g., TAM, UTAUT), this study shifts the analytical lens to institutional governance and its marketing implications, framing academic trust as a vital strategic brand asset that drives organizational legitimacy and student behavioral intentions. We propose and empirically test a multidimensional governance framework consisting of four core pillars: ethical transparency, algorithmic accountability, digital AI literacy, and adaptive AI governance. Utilizing a quantitative research design and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), we analyze survey data from 380 higher education students in Tunisia. The structural model reveals that Adaptive AI Governance is the most powerful predictor of Institutional Trust (β = 0.297, p < 0.001), followed by Algorithmic Accountability (β = 0.258, p < 0.001) and Ethical Transparency (β = 0.231, p < 0.001), while AI Literacy has a smaller but significant effect (β = 0.137, p = 0.006). Institutional Trust, in turn, exhibits an exceptionally strong positive relationship with Perceived Institutional Ethicality (β = 0.741, p < 0.001). Together, trust and ethicality explain 61.2% of the variance in students' behavioral intentions toward sustainable AI use, with perceived ethicality acting as a significant partial mediating mechanism (β_indirect = 0.337, p < 0.001). Beyond pedagogical compliance, these findings demonstrate that robust governance directly enhances institutional brand equity, student attraction, and procedural legitimacy. We outline strategic recommendations for university marketers and educators to co-create proactive, values-led learning ecosystems that strengthen academic reputation in the digital era.

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative social robots (GSRs) powered by large language models offer new possibilities for personalized tutoring in higher education, but also introduce risks related to misinformation, missing transparency, or reinforcing incorrect student responses. Prior work identified knowledge-based design (KBD) requirements that define the information GSRs need to tutor responsibly and effectively in higher education. Methods In this paper, we operationalized selected KBD requirements in the Reachy Mini robot platform through system prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, and stateful prompt orchestration. We present Teachy Mini, a GSR tutoring prototype based on these design requirements. To test the system, we conducted a preliminary evaluation study. Participants ( N = 24) completed a robot-guided learning session about research methodologies. They learned with either Teachy Mini or a robot without the KBD features. Results and discussion Teachy Mini was perceived as significantly more aligned with responsible tutoring behavior than the robot in the control condition. In addition, a qualitative analysis showed that Teachy Mini more often used context-sensitive explanations, Socratic questions, and personalized feedback compared to the robot without KBD features. No significant between-condition differences were found in system acceptance, intrinsic motivation, or learning effectiveness, although exploratory analyses suggested a positive effect of KBD on objective learning gains when accounting for learner preferences. Furthermore, an exploratory path model suggested that the robot’s perceived responsible behavior may be associated with learner motivation and acceptance. Overall, the study suggests that KBD can meaningfully shape responsible robot tutoring behavior. However, the effect of KBD on learner experiences requires further research.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates educational documentation, workplace management, clinical screening, and other institutional processes that affect neurodivergent people. This article argues that prevailing approaches to AI governance, disability rights, and cognitive liberty may fail to make visible a category of harm that is structural, cumulative, and experienced through persistent misrecognition rather than a single identifiable adverse event. I call this problem the Invisible Harm Doctrine. Drawing on scholarship on autistic camouflaging, autistic burnout, sensory and perceptual difference, algorithmic management, automation bias, AI fairness, and emerging neurorights, the article develops a normative account of how apparently neutral AI-mediated systems may reproduce neurotypical assumptions about communication, attention, behavior, and performance. It draws on Epistemic Parallax, a construct developed in the author’s prior published work, as a conceptual account of the mismatch between the normative frames through which systems classify behavior and the lived contexts those classifications purport to assess. The article proposes neurodivergent cognitive liberty as a complementary normative formulation, not an existing legal right and not a replacement for present neurorights frameworks. It states the principal objections to the doctrine and responds to them, and it concludes by identifying research, design, and governance questions necessary to evaluate whether and how these harms can be detected, challenged, and mitigated. The article does not report new primary data, establish clinical efficacy, or propose a ready-to-adopt legal standard.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) has significantly transformed how organizations manage information, develop strategic alternatives, and support managerial decision-making, shifting leadership responsibilities from information gathering toward directing, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated outputs. This transformation raises critical questions concerning the boundaries of human and machine authority, accountability for AI-assisted decisions, and the strategic capabilities required for responsible AI integration. This study aimed to examine the transformation of managerial leadership in AI-assisted decision-making, identify key dimensions of managerial accountability, and synthesize the strategic capabilities necessary for responsible technology integration. A qualitative approach employing an integrative literature review was adopted, drawing on peer-reviewed journal articles, academic books, and official documents published primarily between 2020 and 2026. The selected literature was analyzed through thematic coding and critical comparative analysis. The findings indicated that managerial leadership evolved around three interrelated functions: directing, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated outputs, rather than simply experiencing a reduction in responsibilities through automation. Managerial accountability encompassed four dimensions: clear allocation of responsibility, transparency and traceability, meaningful human oversight, and risk management. These dimensions provided a conceptual basis for maintaining human accountability in AI-assisted decision-making. Furthermore, five strategic capabilities were identified as central to responsible AI integration: AI literacy, knowledge integration, governance capabilities, strategic adaptability, and organizational learning. The study concluded that managerial leadership transformation in the era of generative AI depended not merely on technological adoption but also on the integration of human judgment, robust accountability mechanisms, and adaptive strategic capabilities. These findings contributed to a conceptual framework for responsible AI governance and sustainable organizational adaptation.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Passenger trust plays a critical role in the adoption of autonomous vehicles (AVs), especially in complex traffic environments where system behavior may be difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a framework linking driving characteristics (e.g., acceleration profiles, responsiveness to other road users, maneuvering patterns) with passengers’ emotional responses and perceived safety. The framework examines how adaptive, emotion-aware human–machine interfaces (HMIs) can enhance transparency and comfort by responding to real-time user states such as stress or discomfort. It combines biometric data (e.g., heart rate variability, skin conductance) with self-reported feedback to assess passenger experience in realistic scenarios, with particular emphasis on in-vehicle cues and external indicators contributing to perceived trust. The approach builds on insights from European research projects, including SHOW, AUGMENTED CCAM, DIVERSITY, DIVERSIFY CCAM, DRIVE2theFuture, AWARE2ALL, and ULTIMO, and aligns conceptually with the Horizon Europe project CERTAIN. Rather than presenting experimental results, the paper proposes a conceptual framework and outlines a methodological pathway for its future empirical validation in driving simulation or controlled automated vehicle environments.

AbstractArtificial intelligence [AI] encompasses advanced computational system designed to execute functions that normally depend on human cognitive abilities, such as learning inference problem solving, and decision-making Therapeutic progress in information systems, the expansion of big data and the growth in computing resources have generally facilitated the incorporation of AI into pharmaceutical and health care sectors. This technological integration has promoted strong partnerships between pharma organizations and AI solution providers , learning to a transformation in technical drug development approaches.AI technologies are now applied across various phases pf pharmaceutical research and development, including identification of therapeutic targets, discovery of new drug molecules, formulation development, designing dosage forms, optimization of clinical manufacturing processes, quality management and quality control , and regulatory submissions . In addition, AI facilitates drug repositioning, accelerate research activities, and automates routine process which collectively enhances productivity, accuracy, and efficiency while reducing both time and operational costs. nevertheless, the practical adoption of AI is accompanied by several barriers, including concerns related to data integrity and availability, complex regulatory requirements, ethical and privacy issues, the limited explainability of AI algorithms, and the shortage of trained professionals with domain expertise. This review aims to explore the contribution of artificial intelligence, particularly artificial neural networks and other AI- based approaches, in pharmaceutical development. It also focuses on the key benefits, existing challenges, and future opportunities, providing insights into how AI can further drive innovation and efficiency in the pharmaceutical industry.Keywords AI, Pharmaceutical Sciences, learning inference problem solving, and decision-making Therapeutic progress.

documents.abstract: This study examined acceptance-related perceptions of ChatGPT among first-year engineering students at a Chilean university. Psychometric analyses included 206 respondents completing all 32 items; inferential analyses included 178 reporting study-related use. Drawing on an extended technology acceptance model as a descriptive framework, we analyzed perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived intelligence, perceived trust, awareness, and adoption intention in relation to gender, school sector, prior academic performance, and usage frequency. Internal consistency estimates were high, but exploratory factor analysis showed incomplete separation of the dimensions, limiting claims of construct validity. After Holm correction, no comparisons by gender, school sector, or prior academic performance remained statistically significant. More frequent use was associated with higher scores across all six dimensions. The findings provide preliminary psychometric evidence and identify usage frequency as the most consistent correlate of acceptance-related perceptions. However, the cross-sectional design does not permit conclusions about directionality, causality, or educational benefits.

European air traffic management (ATM) is facing increasing delays and capacity challenges, necessitating new approaches to automation and human-AI collaboration. This paper examines the SESAR exploratory research projects AISA (AI Situational Awareness Foundation for Advancing Automation) and its continuation, AWARE (Achieving Human-Machine Collaboration with Artificial Situational Awareness), through the lens of Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs). AISA introduced the concept of AI-based situational awareness using knowledge graphs and reasoning engines, while AWARE advances this work with an AI assistant that monitors air traffic controllers’ intent, workload, and interaction to provide tailored support. Although officially classified at low TRL levels, both projects developed and validated components reaching higher maturity, reflecting the need for demonstrable solutions even in early research. The analysis highlights the potential of human-AI teaming to increase safety, capacity, and efficiency in ATM, while emphasising the importance of gradual, validated integration of AI into this safety-critical domain.
topics: Military Command and Control and Network-Centric Warfare

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI (GenAI), is transforming tourism-related tasks and creating new competency requirements for future professionals. This conceptual paper synthesises research on AI competencies and contextualises them within tourism occupations. It proposes the Tourism AI Competency Framework, comprising six domains: (1) AI literacy; (2) AI application in tourism; (3) data and analytical literacy; (4) digital customer experience; (5) human–AI collaboration; and (6) responsible AI use. The framework comprises three developmental levels, progressing from awareness to application and AI-augmented professional practice. The paper argues that AI integration should not be reduced to the addition of a standalone technology course. Instead, curriculum redesign should begin with changes in occupational tasks and translate these changes into competencies, learning outcomes, learning activities, and assessment.
