documents.abstract: The paradigm of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has been developed as a solution for increasing transparency, interpretability, and accountability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models used in autonomous Information Technology (IT) systems. The fast adoption of autonomous AI technologies …

Generative AI can support robotics programming, but students must still evaluate suggestions and justify design decisions. This study examined changes in grit-related learning dispositions and patterns of epistemic activity during instruction using the Cognitive Synergy Framework (CSF). In a mixed-methods study across six West African universities, we randomly allocated 410 undergraduates to CSF-supported or comparison instruction. A categorical-time mixed-effects model analysed 848 Grit in Robotics Programming scores from 351 students across Weeks 11, 13, and 15. Epistemic network analysis examined coded actions from 30 collaborative groups. The reported GRP condition-by-time interaction was significant, Wald χ 2 (2) = 15.02, p < .001. Relative to Week 11, estimated gains were 0.167 points greater under CSF at Week 13 (95% CI [0.059, 0.274]) and 0.213 points greater at Week 15 (95% CI [0.093, 0.333]). With a 0.20-point downward adjustment to imputed CSF scores at both follow-ups, the joint test yielded p = .103. Group-level network trajectories differed by condition (β = 0.09, 95% CI [0.03, 0.15], p = .004). Gains in independent epistemic agency remained untested. Future studies should match instructional support across conditions and assess individual reasoning, evaluative judgement, and knowledge construction on tasks completed without scaffolding.

Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) are reshaping maritime work by relocating safety-critical navigation from ship bridges to Remote Operations Centres (ROCs). This review examines whether research on MASS and ROC operator skills and competencies provides a sufficient basis for assessing their application during remote navigation. A combined bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review identified peer-reviewed studies from Web of Science, Scopus, and Transport Research International Documentation (TRID), with 48 studies included in the qualitative synthesis. The bibliometric analysis shows a fragmented field in which safety and navigation are prominent, while human-element and situation-awareness themes remain less consolidated. The thematic synthesis identified five competency domains: safety-critical cognition, digital-technical and Human–Machine Interface (HMI)-related competencies, reconfigured maritime operational expertise, communication and teamwork in distributed operations, and meta-competencies and adaptive capacity. These domains were interpreted through Endsley’s three-level Situation Awareness (SA) framework to examine how competencies may support perception, comprehension, and projection before decision-making and task execution. Although studies identify many competencies required for ROC operators, they provide much less evidence on how those competencies should be evaluated during safety-critical ROC performance. Future research should examine competency–SA relationships through task- and simulator-based assessment before assuming direct transfer or inadequacy of existing maritime competencies.

Extended Reality (XR) research in education has focused on immersion, presence, engagement, simulation and experiential learning. These perspectives explain immersive learning but do not fully account for the quality of the worlds learners enter. A virtual environment may be visually compelling while remaining pedagogically shallow, weakly structured or ethically unexamined. This study develops and applies an educational adaptation of Secondary World theory to examine AI-supported XR design in teacher education. The study draws on a theory-driven secondary mixed-methods analysis of an intervention involving 140 pre-service teachers working in 24 teams. Participants designed 48 virtual environments across CoSpaces and Minecraft, using ChatGPT for scenarios, learner personas and critique, and Spline for three-dimensional assets. The analysis examined team-level design artefacts, peer feedback, coded records and reflections across seven dimensions: coherence, depth, actionability, consequence, sub-creation, transfer and reflexivity. Four levels of educational world-making were identified: scenic immersion, task-world construction, pedagogical world construction and reflexive Secondary World-making. Most designs remained scenic or task-oriented, while fewer formed coherent pedagogical worlds integrating learner roles, actions, feedback and transfer. CoSpaces tended to support structured sequencing, while Minecraft supported spatial extension and collaborative construction. These patterns reflected platform affordances and design sequence. Generative AI was most strongly associated with higher-level world-making when used to test assumptions, accessibility, learner agency and pedagogical coherence rather than generate content. The study contributes a framework for evaluating XR learning environments beyond immersion and argues that teacher education should prepare future teachers to design, evaluate and critique the educational worlds technology makes possible.

This conceptual paper traces the connection between Jean-Pol Martin’s Learning by Teaching (Lernen durch Lehren, LdL) and the New Human Rights (Neue Menschenrechte, NMR). It takes Martin’s 1985 dissertation on information processing in foreign-language teaching and his 1994 habilitation on the anthropological foundations of the curriculum as historical starting points. The paper makes explicit the normative premise that connects learner agency to institutional justice. If everyone’s basic needs deserve equal consideration, institutions should provide comparable effective opportunities to meet them. Two hypothetical examples, a classroom in which pupils take turns teaching and a municipal consultation, illustrate how access, support and influence determine whether people can meaningfully participate. The supplementary file Der Organismus als Ausgangspunkt contains the German translation of the AI-generated reconstruction by Le Chat that prompted this paper. The translation was prepared by ChatGPT.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming human resource management (HRM) through its applications in recruitment and selection, performance evaluation, employee engagement, learning and development, workforce planning, and talent management. Despite the operational benefits of AI-enabled HRM, employee acceptance remains influenced by concerns regarding algorithmic fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, and the reliability of automated decisions. This study develops and examines a framework explaining how perceived fairness, transparency, and employee confidence contribute to organisational trust and how organisational trust subsequently influences employees’ intention to adopt AI-enabled HRM systems. The study is conceptually grounded in organisational trust theory, organisational justice theory, and technology acceptance perspectives. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design is proposed, with an sample of 160 employees and HR professionals working in Indian organisations. A structured questionnaire based on a five-point Likert scale is used as the proposed measurement instrument. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, construct validity assessment, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression are applied to demonstrate the analysis. The findings indicate that perceived fairness, transparency, and employee confidence positively contribute to organisational trust in AI-enabled HRM. Organisational trust also demonstrates a positive association with employees’ intention to adopt AI-enabled HRM systems. The findings suggest that successful AI adoption in HRM depends not only on technological capability but also on organisational credibility, transparent decision-making, perceived procedural justice, and employee confidence. The study offers implications for Indian organisations seeking to implement responsible, trustworthy, and employee-centred AI-enabled HR practices.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: AI-native development environments are changing how digital products can be created, removing the barrier of human technical effort required to translate defined requirements into functioning software. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), this creates opportunities to participate more directly in digital production without requiring input from service providers. An appointment-based business case developed in an AI-native environment serves as one practical stress test of the implications of service design using Vibe Coding. The analysis distinguishes technical capability from economic sustainability and considers how integrated cloud services, AI computation, credit-based consumption and opaque cost attribution can complicate accountability for users with limited technical expertise. It concludes that a service provider cannot responsibly assume open-ended accountability for a system when its operating costs, dependencies and technical conditions may change beyond the provider's control. Connecting this use case to the industry's shift from Vibe Coding towards causal reasoning models and autonomous AI agents, this exploratory paper proposes quantum computing for the classification and optimisation of factory ontology data and in support of classical machine learning models. For critical manufacturing at scale, where token-based costs, energy use and sustainability goals may require it, quantum computing may provide the relevant evidence to inform and develop better tools that can intelligently manage the reliance of input by autonomous agents and black-box LLMs with that of lower expense deterministic, traditional algorithm-based logic.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Gamified formative assessment, which adds game elements such as points, badges and leaderboards to low-stakes quizzes, is widely promoted as a way of increasing engagement, yet controlled evidence from sub-Saharan African STEM classrooms is scarce. This study tested the effect of gamified formative assessment on cognitive and affective outcomes among Senior Secondary 2 students in Imo State, South-East Nigeria. A pretest–posttest, delayed-posttest quasi-experimental design with a control group was used. Twelve intact Mathematics and Physics classes from 12 schools were randomly assigned to gamified assessment on digital quiz platforms (n = 158) or to non-gamified paper quizzes with the same items and feedback (n = 154) for eight weeks. After controlling for pretest scores, the gamified group outperformed the control group on the posttest, F(1, 309) = 124.13, p < .001, η²p = .29, g = 1.26, and on a delayed retention test four weeks later, F(1, 309) = 59.80, p < .001, g = 0.88. The gamified group also reported higher behavioural, emotional and cognitive engagement (g = 0.84 to 1.15) and intrinsic motivation (g = 0.84), and slightly lower test anxiety (g = −0.23). Gender did not moderate the effect. The findings suggest that gamified formative assessment can improve both achievement and engagement in resource-constrained STEM classrooms, although novelty effects and the short duration warrant caution. Keywords: Gamification; Formative Assessment; Student Engagement; Motivation; STEM Education; Nigeria

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the organisation of work, yet relatively little is known about how the workers closest to the technology interpret its consequences for their own occupations. This study examines how technology practitioners discuss the effects of generative AI on jobs, careers and hiring, and how this discourse changed between January 2023 and September 2026. A new corpus was assembled from Hacker News, a large online forum for software and technology professionals. Keyword retrieval was combined with a zero-shot relevance classifier, which yielded 34,270 comments written by 13,576 contributors with an estimated precision of 85.3% on a held-out random sample. Four topic models, namely LDA, NMF and two BERTopic variants, were compared on coherence, diversity and coverage, and non-negative matrix factorisation with 15 topics provided the best balance. Sentence embeddings were then clustered with k-means to identify broader discourse frames, and the monthly topic composition was segmented with contiguity-constrained hierarchical clustering to detect discourse phases. Six frames emerged, covering corporate layoffs and AI-washing, AI as a tool or a threat to the programming craft, software careers and the junior pipeline, creative and knowledge-work displacement, AI in recruitment, and macro-level automation, economy and society. Labour-related discussion intensified from about 31 to 47 comments per 1,000 AI-related comments. The only robust change point, in May 2025, marks a shift towards layoffs, careers and the entry-level pipeline and away from debates about AI in recruitment, while macro-level debate about automation remained stable. The findings indicate that practitioner attention has turned towards how employers restructure work and entry routes, with implications for human resource management, career guidance and workforce policy.

documents.abstract: As generative AI (GenAI) technologies become increasingly integrated into global workplaces, their implications for individual career development, particularly among internationally mobile professionals, remain underexplored. This study examines the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and expatriates’ career adaptability, as well as three career sustainability-related outcomes: career satisfaction, life satisfaction, and perceived AI-enabled task performance. Grounded in Career Construction Theory, the study conceptualizes human–GenAI collaboration as a contextual resource associated with adaptive career responses. Drawing on data from 361 expatriates, the findings indicate that human–GenAI collaboration is positively associated with career adaptability, which in turn relates positively to these career-related outcomes. The results further show that the relationship between human–GenAI collaboration and career adaptability varies according to expatriates’ AI trust and perceived AI-induced job insecurity. This study contributes to research on career development and human–AI interaction by highlighting the role of digitally mediated work practices in adaptive career processes within global work contexts.

Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical education. However, concerns about its professional, ethical, and psychological implications for future physicians remain insufficiently studied, particularly in resource-constrained settings. This study assessed GenAI-related concerns among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, using the Fear, Anxiety, Mistrust, and Ethics (FAME) scale. Methods A multi-institutional cross-sectional online survey using convenience sampling via online recruitment was conducted among medical students at Palestinian universities between March and April 2026. Data were collected on sociodemographic and academic characteristics, prior GenAI tool use, self-reported level of AI concern, and FAME scores. Non-parametric tests and multiple linear regression were used for analysis. Results Of 399 participants included in the analysis, 96.0% reported using ChatGPT. The median total FAME score was 40 (IQR, 35–45). Median domain scores were highest for Mistrust and Ethics, both with a median score of 11, compared with Fear and Anxiety, both with a median score of 9. Male students had higher Fear and Anxiety scores than female students, but total FAME scores did not differ significantly by gender. In the exploratory adjusted regression model, no sociodemographic, academic, or AI-use variable was independently associated with the total FAME score, and the overall model explained only a small proportion of score variability. Conclusions GenAI use was widespread among Palestinian medical students in the West Bank, Palestine, with higher median scores observed in the mistrust and ethics domains than in fear of professional displacement. None of the variables included in the exploratory multivariable model was independently associated with total FAME score. Structured AI-literacy education addressing ethical reasoning and critical appraisal of AI-generated information may represent a potential educational implication of these findings.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined reported GenAI use for academic work in 2022–23 and reported intention to use GenAI in 2023–24 among 1,021 English-fluent postsecondary students purposively recruited from multiple countries in September 2023. Descriptive statistics and exploratory, unadjusted Pearson chi-square tests examined bivariate associations with gender, primary-language category, and level-of-study category. Overall, 73.1% of participants reported using GenAI for academic work in 2022–23, and 65.6% reported intending to use it in 2023–24. Among GenAI users, 89.5% identified ChatGPT as the tool they used most. Statistically significant but small bivariate associations were found between gender and both outcomes, primary-language category and both outcomes, and graduate-versus-undergraduate category and reported use. No statistically significant association was detected between level-of-study category and reported intention. These findings provide a time-specific account of GenAI engagement within this multinational sample but do not establish population prevalence or independent demographic associations. They are compatible with selected aspects of postplagiarism, which served as an interpretive framework rather than a theory tested by the survey.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems have begun to produce faster and less error-prone results than humans in many domains, from education and health to science and governance. This opinion paper discusses an overlooked cost of this development: error is not merely a deficiency that humans should avoid, but a constitutive experience of learning, discovery, and meaning-making. The paper distinguishes three levels, termed functional perfection, human development, and existential meaning. It argues that technology can deliver major progress at the first level but cannot by itself resolve the other two. Findings from a recent study of a community of AI agents conducting science support this claim in two ways. On the one hand, even machines improve not by eliminating error but by making it visible and correcting it. On the other hand, agents that excel in experimental rigor lag behind humans in choosing significant questions and producing original contributions. After addressing possible objections, the paper proposes implications for education, research, and policy. Its central conclusion is that the education of the future should cultivate not individuals who answer better than AI, but individuals who can ask questions beyond AI’s answers, live with uncertainty, and preserve the right to learn through error.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbots in e-commerce has restructured customer service delivery. However, online shoppers frequently experience pre-purchase decision hesitation due to transaction uncertainties. Grounded in Uncertainty Reduction Theory and Social Response Theory, this study investigates how Conversational AI Responsiveness and Perceived Anthropomorphism mitigate Customer Decision Hesitation through the mediating role of Brand Trust. Data were collected via an online survey from 195 e-commerce consumers in Indonesia who interacted with AI chatbots during their shopping journeys. The empirical framework was evaluated using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. The empirical results reveal that both Conversational AI Responsiveness (β=0.482,p<0.001) and Perceived Anthropomorphism (β=0.325,p<0.001) significantly foster Brand Trust, while directly and indirectly mitigating Customer Decision Hesitation. Furthermore, Brand Trust operates as a vital complementary mediating mechanism (β=-0.395,p<0.001). The structural model explains 51.4 percent of the variance in Brand Trust and 48.7 percent in Customer Decision Hesitation. This research advances Marketing Technology literature by elucidating how humanized AI interactions alleviate choice anxiety, providing strategic guidelines for digital retailers to curb cart abandonment.

Some public-service tasks involve requests for personal information, making a robot's presented role and service behavior relevant to users’ privacy perceptions. We examine professional identity cues and service proactivity in a simulated Chinese government-service setting. Semi-structured interviews ( \(n=17\) ) informed the study design; a pilot study ( \(n=34\) ) checked the manipulations; and a 2×2 within-subjects virtual study ( \(n=36\) ) measured self-reported privacy sensitivity and the depth of simulated disclosure. In the main study, participants reported lower privacy sensitivity with robots presented as having a professional identity, and service proactivity interacted with identity presentation. Interviewees differed in their preferences: some found passive service less intrusive, whereas others valued proactive assistance for anticipating their needs. These findings concern perceptions and choices in a simulation, not the robot's actual institutional authorization or data security. They inform context-sensitive interaction design without treating increased disclosure as a goal or professional appearance as proof of privacy protection.

Despite the rapidly growing popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in universities, this study explores its impact on students’ academic costs at the higher education level. The study focuses on higher education students at public sector universities in the Hazara Division regarding the use of AI tools to minimise their educational costs. The study used quantitative data analysis and techniques in SPSS-26. It checked the reliability and validity of the data and then used regression analysis to meet the study objectives. Findings showed that effective utilisation of AI tools positively impacts students’ overall academic costs. Strategic integration of AI tools significantly contributes to lower academic costs, as shown in the gender-based analysis.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This research seeks to analyze the connection between perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being of employees through a quantitative correlational approach. The emergence of artificial intelligence in the working environment raises worries in regard to job security and the threat of unemployment. Thus, there may be a rise in employment worries and a decrease in employees' mental well-being. The methodology to collect data on employees levels of perceived AI menace, fear of unemployment, and mental well-being is based on surveying them using conventional self-reported questionnaires. Descriptive statistics will be used to analyze the levels of these factors in terms of their means (M) and standard deviations (SD). The reliability analysis is going to be done for checking internal reliability of a research tool using Cronbach's alpha. To measure the relationships between these three variables, a Pearson product-moment correlation will be used. Additionally, a simple linear regression will be run in order to see if perceived threat from AI can predict unemployment anxiety and psychological well-being and if unemployment anxiety can predict psychological well-being. The measurement of psychological well-being is going to be based on the six dimensions introduced by Ryff: autonomy, environmental mastery, personal growth, positive relations with others, purpose in life, and self-acceptance. The results of this study will allow understanding how the way employees view AI being a threat to their jobs relates to worries about unemployment and psychological well-being. All in all, the results of this research can be helpful for realizing the significance of recognizing employees’ concerns in the course of technological changes and encourage businesses to provide adequate support to employees for mitigating job-related uncertainty and reaching psychological well-being.

This study examined influence of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) on cognitive engagement among senior secondary school students in Minna Metropolis, Niger State, Nigeria. Two objectives guided the study, and two research questions were raised and answered. Two null hypotheses were formulated and tested at 0.05 levels of significance. Descriptive survey design was adopted for the study. The population of the study comprised of 3,023 senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State. The sample of the study was 311 senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State which was selected through multi-stage sampling procedure. Influence of Information and Communication Technology on Students’ Cognitive Engagement Questionnaire’ (IICTSCEQ) was used for data collection and it was validated by three experts from the Department of Counselling Psychology, IBBU Lapai. Test re-test method was used to obtain the reliability coefficient and co-efficient-value was 0.82. The data collected were analyzed through the use of Statistical Product for Service Solution (SPSS- version 24). Frequency counts and percentage were used to present the demographic information of the respondents, mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions, simple linear regression was used to test hypotheses 1 and independent sample t-test was used to test hypotheses 2 at 0.05 levels of significance. The findings of the study revealed among others that ICT has a significant positive influence on cognitive engagement of senior secondary school students in Minna Metropolis Niger State; and there is no significant difference between male and female respondents in the influence of ICT on cognitive engagement among senior secondary school students in Minna Metropolis, Niger State. The study concluded that ICT significantly influences the cognitive engagement of senior secondary school students by improving critical thinking to learning. Based on these findings, the researcher recommended that Teachers should combine ICT tools with innovative teaching strategies that promote critical thinking and problem-solving skills to enhance the cognitive engagement of senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State, Nigeria; and School administrators and teachers should ensure that ICT instructional strategies are designed to equally stimulate the cognitive engagement of both male and female senior secondary school students in Minna metropolis, Niger State, Nigeria.

The objective of this study was to synthesize evidence regarding the relationship between the academic use of generative artificial intelligence and self-regulated learning among higher education students in Ecuador. A systematic literature review was conducted, involving a structured web-based search for publications in Spanish and English from the 2023–2026 period. Out of 25 identified records, five publications were selected. The selection process was documented using a diagram adapted from the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and methodological quality was assessed using the MMAT 2018 instrument. The narrative synthesis revealed positive associations between the frequency of generative artificial intelligence use and both learning planning and monitoring. One intervention, which combined three artificial intelligence tools with pedagogical guidance, showed an increase in scores for goal setting and self-monitoring. Self-evaluation was addressed by only a single specific estimate, derived from a study that contained discrepancies in its reported sample size. It was concluded that, among the publications examined, the evidence was more consistent for planning and monitoring than for self-evaluation. Variations in research designs and instruments limited the ability to establish causal links or generalize the findings to the context of higher education in Ecuador.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The transformations resulting from the spread of artificial intelligence in educational environments have opened up new perspectives for the organization of teaching, while simultaneously raising questions about its impact on knowledge construction and students' intellectual autonomy. Given this context, the research aimed to analyze the effects of artificial intelligence and digital tools on learning processes, examining their pedagogical potential, operational limitations, and ethical and social implications. To this end, a qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive study was conducted, based on a literature review of scientific works published in Portuguese between 2019 and 2026, sourced from the SciELO, DOAJ, and Google Scholar databases. The analysis of the literature revealed opportunities for methodological diversification, the personalization of educational experiences, and the enhancement of teaching activities through the use of intelligent systems. Conversely, challenges were identified, including inequalities in access, a lack of digital literacy, algorithmic biases, and risks to authorship and critical thinking. The findings indicate that the integration of technology does not, in itself, guarantee improvements in the quality of learning, as its effects depend on the pedagogical and institutional conditions under which it is implemented. It is therefore concluded that the use of artificial intelligence in education requires qualified pedagogical mediation, human oversight, ethical guidelines, and strategies that preserve the student's role as an active agent—ensuring a convergence between technological innovation and the development of cognitive, reflective, and social competencies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Knowledge that is possesed by enterprise employees and codified and stored in data and knowledge bases is very important part of enterprise intellectual capital. Enterprises in developed countries invested in intellectual capital, undertaking various initiatives and projects of knowledge management. In many enterprises, investments are directed towards knowledge management information systems incorporating artificial intelligence. These intelligent information systems support whole process of knowledge management from acquision through storage, dissemination to application of knowledge. These systems with its subsystems are breafly explained and illustrated in this research.

Legibility in human-robot interaction (HRI) is often described as the property of robot motion that enables an observer to confidently and quickly infer the robot’s intent. Mature frameworks exist for generating legible motion in front of static observers, typically by making the robot’s destination apparent as early as possible. Social robot navigation in public spaces, however, presents a different challenge: pedestrians are themselves in motion, often with divided attention, and must coordinate with the robot in real time. In such encounters, where the robot is ultimately headed may matter less to a pedestrian than how it intends to pass them. This raises two questions: which aspect of intent should legible motion convey, and does legibility remain beneficial when pedestrians are not fully attentive to the robot? We address these questions in the ubiquitous and demanding scenario of hallway navigation, through two controlled user studies comparing multiple legibility formulations implemented within a shared model predictive control framework. Study 1 ( N = 45) compares destination-based and passing-side intent representations, showing that the latter, particularly when adaptively updated, allows for smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than the former. Study 2 ( N = 45) examines the effect of pedestrian attention, demonstrating that legible motion supports smooth human motion even under distraction, although this benefit is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings. Together, these findings suggest that effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with some effects persisting even when human attention is divided. Code is available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI and footage from our experiments at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P5O5BwfcUCo .

In twenty-first-century discourse, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly framed as a system that reduces human behaviour, sentiment, and relationship to pattern recognition, predictive modelling, and data optimization. While this phenomenon is historically unprecedented in its technological architecture, its underlying socio-behavioural mechanics- reducing human subjectivity to structural metrics and formulaic calculations- are far from new. This paper positions the Regency novels of Jane Austen as an anticipatory critique of the algorithmic reduction of human interiority. Operating during the onset of the Industrial Revolution and the rise of early capitalist market logic, Austen observed a societal impulse to treat human relationships as transactional math. By closely reading Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, and Emma, this paper explores how Austen's "calculating characters" function as early analogues to predictive algorithms and large language models, showing that her ultimate defense of the "uncalculating" mind serves as a vital framework for preserving human agency against automated optimization.

The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across industries is fundamentally transforming organizational structures, decision-making processes, workforce dynamics, and leadership practices. As intelligent systems increasingly automate routine tasks and augment human capabilities, leaders face new challenges related to strategy, workforce development, ethics, organizational transformation, and innovation management. Traditional leadership approaches, while still valuable, are often insufficient for navigating the complexities of AI-driven environments characterized by rapid technological change, uncertainty, and continuous disruption. This article explores the emerging competencies required for leadership in AI-enabled organizations, focusing on resilience, adaptability, strategic foresight, digital literacy, ethical stewardship, and human-centered innovation. Drawing upon contemporary research and global examples, the article examines how organizations can cultivate leadership capabilities that balance technological advancement with organizational sustainability, employee well-being, and long-term value creation. It argues that successful AI leadership is not merely about managing technology but about leading people through technological transformation.

This research examines the topic of “Legal Liability for Harm Caused by Artificial Intelligence and Algorithms: A Comparative Study of Criminal, Civil, and Administrative Liability in the European Union and the United Arab Emirates.” It aims to explain the legal framework governing the use and processing of data and information, and to identify the harm that may result from algorithmic outputs, particularly violations of privacy, damage to reputation, the spread of misleading information, fraud, identity theft, and the unlawful disclosure of personal data. The research uses a descriptive, analytical, and comparative approach. It describes and analyses relevant legal provisions and compares the legal protection measures, oversight mechanisms, and penalties in the European Union and the United Arab Emirates. The study also examines civil liability, including its main elements and the conditions for compensation for material and non-material damage. It addresses administrative liability in terms of regulatory obligations, supervision, and penalties. In addition, it examines criminal liability, including the elements of a crime and the attribution of criminal acts to natural or legal persons, depending on the nature of the act. The findings show that the involvement of multiple parties in developing, operating, and using artificial intelligence systems makes liability more complex. The mere fact that harm results from an algorithmic output is not sufficient to establish liability. It is necessary to determine whether an unlawful act occurred, whether damage was caused, whether there is a causal link between the act and the damage, and whether the legally required criminal intent exists. The study recommends updating legislation governing liability for harm caused by artificial intelligence, strengthening transparency and human oversight, improving the preservation of digital evidence and the proof of causation, clarifying the obligations of developers, providers, and users, and enhancing cooperation between regulatory and judicial authorities. These measures would help protect rights and achieve a balance between technological innovation and legal accountability.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Total Worker Health® (TWH) approach has broadened the factors recognized as contributing to worker health, safety, and well-being. Many work conditions attended to by the TWH approach, however, are shaped by power relations between workers and employers, and are reinforced by regulation and social, economic, and political norms. Recognizing that concepts of power and power relations can be a difficult topic for occupational health and safety professionals and researchers to discuss, this paper introduces the concepts of structural and psychological empowerment, and, after describing validated tools used to measure these concepts, assesses the extent to which these concepts are captured in survey instruments used in TWH research. METHODS: This study uses a narrative literature review to identify validated instruments used to measure structural and psychological empowerment. The concepts and instruments are then compared to items in the NIOSH WellBQ survey, the Healthy Work Survey, and the Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire III. RESULTS: The NIOSH WellBQ, Healthy Work Survey, and Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire III each capture some elements of structural and psychological empowerment, but require supplemental questions to capture all elements of these concepts. CONCLUSIONS: Occupational health and safety professionals and researchers must become more comfortable talking about power and power relations because changing these workplace characteristics may improve worker health, safety, and well-being through many elements of the TWH approach.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: The article provides a theoretical rationale for the need to develop meta-skills as a regulatory level of human personal, educational and professional capability amid the spread of digital technologies and generative artificial intelligence.The aim of the study is to clarify the meaning of the concept of "meta-skills", identify the factors that necessitate their development, and construct a structural and functional model of meta-skills for a hybrid digital and mental environment.The methods of theoretical analysis, comparative analysis of international competence frameworks, conceptual synthesis and modelling were applied.Meta-skills are proposed to be understood as an integrated higher-order capacity that enables the conscious acquisition, regulation, verification, transfer and ethically responsible application of technical and professional skills and social and communication skills in new contexts.Six interrelated components are identified: metacognitive and learning, critical and informational, self-regulatory, adaptive and transfer, social and communicative, and digital and ethical.It is substantiated that the system's fundamental mechanism is the capacity for lifelong learning, while its effectiveness is manifested in the preservation of human agency, the ability to verify AI-generated results, manage attention and emotional load, transfer ways of acting across situations, and take responsibility for making the final decision.Principles for developing meta-skills and criteria for assessing them are identified that are suitable for designing educational and professional programmes.The practical significance of the findings lies in the possibility of incorporating the proposed cycle into the training of specialists in various fields.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for sustainability assessment and decision support, yet their judgments may depend on the selected model and on how the task is defined. We compare 13 locally executed open-weight LLMs on 80 author-written sustainability scenarios using three prompt families that ask which actor should be responsible, bear the costs, or initiate action. Each model answered at two temperature settings with 100 repetitions, producing 624,000 deposited outputs, of which 610,708 contain a complete score vector. Scores were analyzed as relative actor support after removing each response’s overall level. Within this instrument, the cost prompt family produced the highest cross-model disagreement, exceeding both responsibility and catalyst by 7.37 points (question-cluster 95% intervals 5.56−9.15 and 5.38−9.36, describing variation across these 80 scenarios). It also produced the most lead-actor disagreement and the lowest full consensus. Moving from catalyst to cost reduced relative support for government and increased it for individuals and firms; moving from cost to responsibility largely reversed this pattern. These differences exceeded temperature-setting differences and persisted under model exclusion, alternative score transformations and tie rules, missing-response checks, and stems without explicit cost wording. Exploratory category patterns are conditional on uneven item coverage. Secondary rationale-language comparisons show the same within-model ordering but not the most cross-model variation under cost. Operational use should disclose model, prompt, and temperature choices; compare plausible alternatives; repeat generations; and refer high-disagreement judgments for human deliberation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: In the contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem, foundation models are increasingly deployed under AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS) schemes characterized by high technical opacity, technological concentration, and limited external auditing capability over governance, training, and internal operational processes. Under these conditions, traditional ethical oversight approaches that focus exclusively on corporate governance or on internal model inspection become insufficient to ensure effective control over AI systems deployed in real-world contexts. This work proposes a pragmatic operational assurance framework inspired by Zero-Trust principles from cybersecurity, which shifts effective auditing efforts toward the application layer, where risk acquires observable, contextualized, and operationally verifiable properties. The proposal articulates two complementary evaluation levels: a black-box evaluation aimed at characterizing general behaviors, vulnerabilities, and risky capabilities of foundation models through conversational scanning, and a grey-box evaluation focused on the operational contextualization of risk within the actual deployment environment of the audited application. The framework incorporates mechanisms to move from general, CVSS-inspired severity metrics toward contextualized operational risk assessments that take into account user profiles, industrial domains, and organizational knowledge. In addition, the proposal strengthens practical auditability through digitally signed explainability reports (signed XAI reports), designed to support verifiable traceability, continuous monitoring, and operational accountability in LLM-based sociotechnical systems.

Mahasiswa Akuntansi Universitas Nias sebagai calon tenaga profesional di bidang akuntansi dan keuangan perlu memiliki kemampuan mengambil keputusan keuangan secara rasional dan tepat. Namun, dalam proses pengambilan keputusan, individu tidak selalu bertindak sepenuhnya berdasarkan informasi objektif. Bias kognitif, seperti anchoring bias, overconfidence bias, dan confirmation bias, dapat memengaruhi cara seseorang menerima, mengolah, dan menilai informasi keuangan. Studi ini bertujuan mengetahui sejauh mana tiga jenis bias kognitif, yakni anchoring bias, overconfidence bias, dan confirmation bias, memengaruhi ketepatan keputusan keuangan manajerial mahasiswa Akuntansi Universitas Nias. Pendekatan yang dipakai adalah kuantitatif asosiatif. Data primer dihimpun melalui kuesioner skala Likert lima poin yang memuat 30 butir pernyataan berbasis empat skenario kasus keuangan manajerial, dan diisi oleh 35 mahasiswa yang dipilih dengan teknik purposive sampling. Data dianalisis menggunakan statistik deskriptif, uji kualitas instrumen, uji asumsi klasik, dan regresi linear berganda. Hasil menunjukkan anchoring bias memiliki koefisien positif tetapi tidak signifikan terhadap ketepatan keputusan (B = 0,450; p = 0,055), sedangkan overconfidence bias (B = −0,272; p = 0,447) dan confirmation bias (B = 0,066; p = 0,770) juga tidak berpengaruh signifikan. Secara simultan, ketiga bias tersebut tidak berpengaruh signifikan terhadap ketepatan keputusan (F = 1,926; p = 0,146) dengan R² sebesar 0,157. Kesimpulan dari penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa variasi ketepatan keputusan dalam sampel lebih banyak berkaitan dengan faktor lain di luar model.

The growing accessibility of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has expanded opportunities for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to automate routine cognitive work and support managerial decisions. This article examines the potential influence of GenAI use on operational efficiency and decision-making quality through a directed integrative literature review. Eight core sources comprising peer-reviewed studies and international institutional reports published between 2023 and 2026 were analyzed using thematic synthesis. The analysis identifies three major mechanisms: faster content and information processing, broader generation of business alternatives, and improved knowledge accessibility for resource-constrained firms. Evidence from professional writing and customer-service settings indicates productivity gains under specific task conditions, while OECD survey results suggest self-reported benefits among GenAI-using SMEs. However, findings from large organizations and selected countries cannot be generalized automatically to Indonesian MSMEs. The quality of managerial decisions still depends on data accuracy, human verification, workers’ digital skills, and privacy safeguards. A practical implementation framework is proposed to connect low-risk pilots, performance indicators, and accountable human oversight. The article concludes that GenAI should be treated as a complementary decision-support capability rather than a substitute for managerial judgment.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Nigerian industrial revolution has progressed through stages of development in different periods (eras). The requirement for operator interface in the distributed control system was fulfilled by Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA). Operator station enabled information systems automation to enhance enterprise resource Integration which enables better strategization to overcome profit squeeze and liquidation. The Programmable Logic Controller provided solution to sequence automation and fast reaction systems where scan times, sequences and event recording are required. Since 1971, the distributed control system has undergone progressive advancement, some of which include: Integration of Microprocessor, Human-Machine interface, Networked Systems, Modular design, integration with Enterprise Resource Planning along with manufacturing execution systems and Internet of Things (IoTs) which enables adoption of industrial procedures: Data Analytics, Cloud Computing, Edge Computing and Cyber- security Protection. Integration of Digital Twins, Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence will make Distributed Control Systems smarter, more efficient and adaptable with many benefits. In Nigeria, the integration of advanced technologies such as Artificial Intelligence into the Distributed Control Systems will enhance efficiency, greater productivity and higher product quality resulting in reduced costs and increased profits. The Nigerian Government is therefore encouraged to overcome the challenges and fully implement artificial intelligence in Nigeria.

Rapid technological change raises an urgent question for higher education: how can universities prepare students for workplaces that may change substantially before they graduate? During several years of study, professional tools and expectations can develop faster than curricula are updated, leaving graduates to acquire essential practical skills after entering employment. The rise of artificial intelligence (AI) makes this challenge more pressing. Online courses and self-directed learning also raise questions about the value of investing in a university qualification when alternative routes offer more immediate professional training. If universities cannot demonstrate how their programmes support professional capability, they risk weakening their appeal to prospective students. This study examines the perceived gap between university preparation and workplace requirements, exploring how participants understand the contribution of educational credentials and practical experience to their professional development. It draws on 35 personal, semi-structured interviews with purposively selected participants from diverse professional and educational backgrounds. Interview material was analysed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by MAXQDA, with curriculum preferences reported separately as descriptive counts. Participants described acquiring changing technologies through work and continued learning. Their responses distinguished the value of qualifications in opening opportunities from the practical capability needed to perform effectively. AI supported faster production, but its use required independent judgement and verification. Universities need to make the practical value of higher education visible throughout students’ learning, while developing the capacity to keep learning as workplace demands change.
topics: Information Systems Education and Curriculum Development

documents.abstract: Tourists abroad routinely face short, consequential service encounters: an inflated taxi fare, a pharmacy visit in an unfamiliar language, a room that does not match the booking. Research on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in tourism has concentrated on how such systems help travellers plan, choose and delegate decisions, and on how AI support during a trip shapes confidence and satisfaction. Separately, research in language education, health-professions education and workplace training shows that rehearsal with simulated counterparts can build skills, although transfer of those skills to real settings is conditional rather than automatic. This conceptual article brings these streams together for the tourist. It proposes the AI-Assisted Travel Rehearsal (ATR) model, an iterative cycle in which travellers rehearse anticipated encounters with general-purpose conversational AI before and during a trip, receive minimal AI support in real encounters, and reflect on each encounter to plan the next rehearsal. Drawing on social cognitive theory, experiential learning theory, the transactional model of stress and coping, scaffolding and fading, and transfer-of-training research, the article specifies a mechanism linking rehearsal to mastery experience, situational self-efficacy and behavioural capability, conditional transfer, and progressive AI fading. Its central claim, the Self-Fading AI Hypothesis, holds that well-designed AI support should reduce travellers' reliance on AI in real encounters without loss of independent performance; reduced AI use alone is not treated as evidence of autonomy. The article states six propositions with explicit conditions of support, identifies which can be tested confirmatorily, and proposes a randomised, actively controlled classroom experiment with AI-unavailable and AI-available transfer tasks, followed by a multilevel field study of first-time international travellers. No empirical results are reported.
keywords: transactional model of stress and coping
